Probably the _Haledj_ of Forskal (p. xcvi. Flor. Ægypt. Arab.), "lignum tenax, durum, obscuri generis." The Bres. Edit, has "ákúl"=teak wood, vulg. "Sáj."

Footnote 286:

The knocker ring is an invention well known to the Romans.

Footnote 287:

Arab. "Sadr"; the place of honour; hence the "Sudder Adawlut" (Supreme Court) in the Anglo-Indian jargon.

Footnote 288:

Arab. "Ahlan wa sahlan wa marhabá," the words still popularly addressed to a guest.

This may mean "liquid black eyes"; but also, as I have noticed, that the lashes were long and thick enough to make the eyelids appear as if Kohl-powder had been applied to the inner rims.

A slight parting between the two front incisors, the upper only, is considered a beauty by Arabs; why it is hard to say except for the racial love of variety. "Sughr" (Thugr) in the text means, primarily, the opening of the mouth, the gape: hence the front teeth.

_i.e._ makes me taste the bitterness of death, "bursting the gall-bladder" (Marárah) being our "breaking the heart."

Almost needless to say that forbidden doors and rooms form a _lieu commun_ in Fairie: they are found in the Hindu Katha Sarit Sagara and became familiar to our childhood by "Bluebeard."

Footnote 293:

Lit. "apply Kohl to my eyes," even as Jezebel "painted her face," in Heb. put her eyes in painting (2 Kings ix., 30).

Arab. "Al-Barkúk," whence our older "Apricock." Classically it is "Burkúk" and Pers. for Arab. "Mishmish," and it also denotes a small plum or damson. In Syria the "side next the sun" shows a glowing red flush.

Arab. "Hazáṙ" (in Persian, a thousand)=a kind of mocking bird.

Some Edit. make the doors number a hundred, but the Princesses were forty and these coincidences, which seem to have significance and have none save for Arab symmetromania, are common in Arab stories.

Arab. "Májúr": hence possibly our "mazer," which is popularly derived from Masarn, a maple.

Footnote 298:

A compound scent of ambergris, musk and aloes.

Footnote 299:

The ends of the bridle-reins forming the whip

The flying horse is Pegasus which is a Greek travesty of an Egyptian myth developed in India.

Footnote 301:

The Bres. Edit. wrongly says "the seventh."

Arab. "Sharmutah" (plur. Sharámít) from the root Sharmat, to shred, a favourite Egyptian word also applied in vulgar speech to a strumpet, a punk, a piece. It is also the popular term for strips of jerked or boucaned meat hung up in the sun to dry, and classically called "Kadíd."

Arab. "Izár," the man's waist-cloth opposed to the Ridá or shoulder-cloth, is also the sheet of white calico worn by the poorer Egyptian women out of doors and covering head and hands. See Lane (M. E., chapt. i). The rich prefer a "Habárah" of black silk, and the poor, when they have nothing else, use a bed-sheet.

_i.e._ "My dears."

Footnote 305:

Arab. "Lá tawákhizná:" lit. "do not chastise (or blame) us;" the pop. expression for, "excuse (or pardon) us."

Arab. "Maskhút," mostly applied to change of shape as man enchanted to monkey, and in vulgar parlance applied to a statue (of stone, etc.). The list of metamorphoses in Al-Islam is longer than that known to Ovid. Those who have seen Petra, the Greek town of the Haurán and the Roman ruins in Northern Africa will readily detect the basis upon which these stories are built. I shall return to this subject in The City of Iram (Night cclxxvi.) and The City of Brass (dlxvii.).

A picturesque phrase enough to express a deserted site, a spectacle familiar to the Nomades and always abounding in pathos to the citizens.

Footnote 308:

The olden "Harem" (or gynæceum, Pers. Zenanah, Serraglio): Harím is also used by synecdoche for the inmates; especially the wife.

Footnote 309:

The pearl is supposed in the East to lose 1% per ann. of its splendour and value.

Footnote 310:

Arab. "Fass," properly the bezel of a ring; also a gem cut _en cabochon_ and generally the _contenant_ for the _contenu_.

Footnote 311:

Arab. "Mihráb"=the arch-headed niche in the Mosque-wall facing Meccah-wards. Here, with his back to the people and fronting the Ka'abah or Square House of Meccah (hence called the "Kiblah"=direction of prayer), stations himself the Imám, antistes or fugleman, lit. "one who stands _before_ others;" and his bows and prostrations give the time to the congregation. I have derived the Mihrab from the niche in which the Egyptian God was shrined: the Jews ignored it, but the Christians preserved it for their statues and altars. Maundrell suggests that the empty niche denotes an invisible God. As the niche (symbol of Venus) and the minaret (symbol of Priapus) date only from the days of the tenth Caliph, Al-Walid (A.H. 86-96=105-115), the Hindus charge the Moslems with having borrowed the two from their favourite idols—The Linga-Yoni or Cunnus-phallus (Pilgrimage ii. 140), and plainly call the Mihrab a Bhaga=Cunnus (Dabistan ii. 152.) Arab. "Kursi," a stool of palm-fronds, etc., ❌-shaped (see Lane's illustration, Nights i., 197), before which the reader sits. Good Moslems will not hold the Holy Volume below the waist nor open it except when ceremonially pure. Englishmen in the East should remember this, for to neglect the "Adab al-Kúran" (respect due to Holy Writ) gives great scandal.

Footnote 313:

Mr. Payne (i. 148) quotes the German Zuckerpüppchen.

Footnote 314:

The Persian poets have a thousand conceits in praise of the "mole," (Khál or Shámah) for which Hafiz offered "Samarkand and Bokhara" (they not being his, as his friends remarked). Another "topic" is the flight of arrows shot by eyelashes.

Arab. "Suhá" a star in the Great Bear introduced only to balance "wushát"=spies, enviers, enemies, whose "evil eye" it will ward off.

Footnote 316:

In Arab tales beauty is always "soft-sided," and a smooth skin is valued in proportion to its rarety.

The myrtle is the young hair upon the side-face.

This is regular formula when speaking of Guebres.

Arab. "Faráiz"; the orders expressly given in the Koran which the reader will remember, is Uncreate and Eternal. In India "Farz" is applied to injunctions thrice repeated; and "Wájib" to those given twice over. Elsewhere scanty difference is made between them.

The latter, according to some commentators, was the voice of the Archangel Gabriel crying "Die all of you" (Koran, chapts. vii. xviii., etc.). We shall hear more of it in the "City of many-coloured Iram." According to some, Salih, a mysterious Badawi prophet, is buried in the Wady al-Shaykh of the so-called Sinaitic Peninsula.

Arab. "Shuhadá"; highly respected by Moslems as by other religionists; although their principal if not only merit seems as a rule to have been intense obstinacy and devotion to one idea for which they were ready to sacrifice even life. The Martyrs-category is extensive including those killed by falling walls; victims to the plague, pleurisy and pregnancy; travellers drowned or otherwise lost when journeying honestly, and chaste lovers who die of "broken hearts" _i.e._ impaired digestion. Their souls are at once stowed away in the crops of green birds where they remain till Resurrection Day, "eating of the fruits and drinking of the streams of Paradise," a place however, whose topography is wholly uncertain. Thus the young Prince was rewarded with a manner of anti-Purgatory, a preparatory heaven.

Arab. "Su 'ubán:" the Badawin give the name to a variety of serpents all held to be venomous; but in tales the word, like "Tannín." expresses our "dragon" or "cockatrice."

She was ashamed to see the lady doing servile duty by rubbing her feet. This _massage_, which B. de la Brocquière describes in 1452 as "kneading and pinching," has already been noticed. The French term is apparently derived from the Arab. "Mas-h."

Alluding to the Most High Name, the hundredth name of God, the Heb. Shem hamphorash, unknown save to a favoured few who by using it perform all manner of miracles.

_i.e._ the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean.

_i.e._ Settled by the Koran.

The uglier the old woman the better procuress she is supposed to make. See the Santa Verdiana in Boccaccio v., 10. In Arab. "Ajuz" (old woman) is highly insulting and if addressed to an Egyptian, whatever be her age she will turn fiercely and resent it. The polite term is Shaybah (Pilgrimage iii., 200).

# A Close Reading of the Opening of *The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night* (Burton, 1885)

---

## 1. What Happens, Scene by Scene

The book opens with a paratextual apparatus—epigraphs in Latin, Italian, French, and Arabic—whose cumulative effect is to position the Nights as a text of unrivalled cultural prestige and moral latitude. Then comes Burton's own Foreword, a long personal essay explaining his methodology: he will translate fully, faithfully, preserving the rhymed prose (*saj'a*), the formulaic openings and closings of each night, the poetry, and—crucially—every obscene or scatological passage, on the grounds that expurgation falsifies the work and that the text is an anthropological document as much as a literary one.

The narrative itself begins with an anonymous narrative voice invoking the usual pious formulae ("In the Name of Allah, the Compassionating, the Compassionate!") and then enters the frame-tale of **King Shahryar** and his brother **Shah Zaman**. Shahryar, ruler of the Islands of India and China, sends his Wazir to summon his younger brother, Shah Zaman, King of Samarcand. On the journey home, Shah Zaman discovers his own wife in flagrante with a black cook; he kills them both, and travels to his brother in a state of existential horror. Shahryar, seeing his brother's despondency, eventually extracts the truth—then discovers, by spying from a lattice window, that his own wife is equally faithless: she too is in the garden with a black slave, and she is not alone; ten concubines and ten Mamelukes are engaged in a full-scale orgy. Shahryar flies into a murderous rage, kills his wife and concubines, and declares that every woman he marries shall be deflowered at night and killed at dawn.

This policy of nightly marriage and morning execution continues for three years, depopulating Baghdad of eligible women. When the Wazir (whose name, **Shahrazad**, is withheld for the moment) is ordered to bring a bride as usual, he cannot find one. He returns home in despair. His elder daughter, **Shahrazad** (called Scheherazade in later tradition), overhears his lament and offers herself as bride, declaring her intention to survive the first night and each subsequent night by telling stories that will hold the King's attention until dawn. Her younger sister, **Dunyazad**, is to be present as listener. The Wazir resists—invoking, as a warning, the tale of the **Bull and the Ass**, in which a donkey's well-meant advice to a bull results in the donkey being worked to death in the bull's place. The point is that counsel to the powerful is dangerous. Shahrazad insists. The Wazir capitulates.

On the wedding night, Shahrazad sends for Dunyazad, who asks for a story to pass the hours. Shahrazad begins the **Tale of the Trader and the Jinni**: a merchant accidentally kills a jinni's son with a date-stone, and the jinni demands his life. The merchant pleads for time to settle his affairs and returns a year later, whereupon three old men each offer to tell stories in exchange for a third of the merchant's blood. The **First Shaykh** tells of a gazelle who is actually his enchantress wife, transformed for her infidelity. The **Second Shaykh** tells of two dogs who are his brothers, also transformed by a jinniyah. The **Third Shaykh** tells of a mule who is his wife, similarly punished. The stories satisfy the jinni, who releases the merchant.

Dunyazad then asks for another tale, and Shahrazad begins the **Fisherman and the Jinni**: a poor fisherman casts his net four times a day (as Burton has earlier explained he himself lived, laboring in West Africa and South America). On the fourth cast he捞上 a sealed copper jar. When he opens it, a vast jinni emerges who was imprisoned by Solomon and who now intends to kill his liberator. The fisherman tricks the jinni back into the jar by questioning how so enormous a being could fit inside so small a container; the jinni re-enters to demonstrate, and the fisherman re-seals the jar and hurls it into the sea. The jinni swears, in exchange for his freedom, to help the fisherman. He directs him to a magical lake containing four coloured fishes—one white, one red, one yellow, one blue—each of which, when delivered to the Sultan, proves to be a transformed citizen of a city whose story the fisherman has set in motion.

From this point the narrative spirals outward. The **Wazir Duban** cures King Yunan of leprosy by means of a hollow bat and a ball, transmitting the medicine through the king's palm during a game of polo. A jealous Wazir convinces the king that Duban must be a poisoner; Duban is executed, but his severed head proves his point by reciting verses, and the poisoned king falls dead. Then come embedded tales: King Sindibad and his falcon (the falcon saves the king from a poisoned tree but is killed for the act of salvation); the Husband and the Parrot (a parrot's truthful report of its mistress's infidelity is disbelieved and the parrot killed); and the Prince and the Ogress (a prince discovers his wife is a ghoul, but is ensorcelled into a creature who is half-man, half-stone). This last tale connects to an **Ensorcelled Prince** in an underground palace who is the son of King Mahmud, Lord of the Black Islands; his wife, a sorceress, has transformed him, transformed the city into four mountains surrounding a magical tarn, and transformed the citizens into fishes of four colours. The Prince's narrative is interrupted by dawn.

Further tales follow in rapid succession: the **Porter and the Three Ladies of Baghdad**, which begins as pure comedy—a Porter is hired to carry an enormous amount of shopping for a beautiful veiled woman, and finds himself in a palatial house with three sisters who entertain him with wine, indecent wordplay, and physical horseplay (slapping, throwing flowers, the Porter being quizzed on anatomical terminology). Into this domestic comedy arrive three **Kalandars** (mendicant ascetics), all blind of the left eye, and then the Caliph Harun al-Rashid himself, travelling incognito with Ja'afar and Masrur. The evening's entertainments include the spectacle of the two **black bitches**—the eldest sister's sisters, transformed by a grateful serpent-Jinniyah—and the songs sung by the sisters, which move the company to tears. The Caliph, unable to contain his curiosity about the bitches and the scarred bodies he sees, causes the ladies to threaten execution. Only when the eldest lady's tale is told does the full history emerge: how she and her sisters were wronged, scattered, and how the two elder sisters were thrown into the sea by their younger sibling (the present lady of the house) after a voyage, and how the Jinniyah punished them. The tales of the three Kalandars also emerge: the first prince lost his eye and beard to a usurping Wazir after his father's assassination; the second prince was transformed into an ape by a jinni after kicking an enchanted alcove and was eventually restored by a princess; the third prince, Ajib, killed the horseman on the Magnet Mountain (the very act prophesied in his own horoscope), fell in love with an underground youth whose life he accidentally ended with a knife, and was finally punished for opening the fortieth door of a magical palace. The three are revealed as princes and are married to the three sisters. The Caliph punishes or rewards everyone accordingly.

## 2. Characters: Who Acts and What Drives Them

**King Shahryar.** His driving force is outrage—a righteous fury that is entirely legitimate in its personal origins but produces a policy of state violence that the narrative ultimately indicts. His character arc moves from injured husband to serial executioner, a trajectory the text presents without explicit moral commentary, letting the accumulating bodies—thousands of women, depopulated Baghdad—speak for themselves. His curiosity, which eventually overrides his murderous routine, is what saves Shahrazad.

**Shah Zaman.** His role is subsidiary but structurally essential: he is the mirror in which Shahryar sees his own reflection. His horror at his wife's infidelity is the catalyst for the brothers' joint journey, and his recovery upon seeing Shahryar's even greater cuckoldry establishes the moral equivalence that drives the King toward madness. He is passive, grief-stricken, and effectively disappears after the frame-tale is established.

**Shahrazad.** She is the book's organizing principle. Her motivation is complex: she speaks of being "a ransom for the virgin daughters of Moslems," which is a public-spirited, even feminist motive, but she is also driven by intellectual pride—she has read a thousand books of history and literature and wishes to prove that knowledge can defeat power. Her method is not bravery but performance: she times her stories to end at dawn, withholding the climaxes of tales to ensure that the King will spare her for the sake of hearing the conclusion. She is, in effect, a professional storyteller who understands the power of narrative suspense as a survival mechanism. She is also, as Burton's Foreword makes clear, the author's own surrogate—another solitary scholar using textual labour to survive a hostile environment.

**The Wazir (Shahrazad's father).** His characteristic mode is anxiety and paternal love combined with practical wisdom. He resists Shahrazad's plan, offers the parable of the Bull and the Ass to discourage her, and even threatens her with the merchant's beating of his wife. His capitulation is not resignation but trust: he has exhausted all other options, and his daughter's confidence inverts the usual power relation between father and child. He is the executor of the King's executions, which makes his position one of daily complicity.

**The Porter.** He functions as the reader's surrogate—naive, curious, physically present, sexually excited, slapped about for his anatomical wordplay. His desire is entirely embodied: he wants to stay, to eat, to drink, to touch the women. His willingness to submit to the "condition" that no questions be asked, and his immediate breaking of it, embody the reader's own predicament: enticed by a narrative that promises pleasure but warns against inquiry.

**The Three Kalandars.** Each is defined by his loss: an eye, a beard, a throne, a beloved, a chance at redemption. Their stories form a catalogue of ways in which fate, desire, and rash action converge to destroy what is most precious. They are not fully rounded characters but experiential nodes—each represents a different relationship to Fortune. The First Kalandar's story is about betrayal by those closest to you (his cousin, his uncle's son); the Second's is about the dangers of intellectual arrogance (kicking the alcove); the Third's is about the inevitability of prophecy (Ajib kills the youth exactly as predicted, by accident).

**The Three Ladies.** The eldest is the dominant personality—organised, wealthy, sexually experienced, capable of both great cruelty (whipping her transformed sisters daily) and great hospitality. The second (the Portress) is defined by her wound—her back bears permanent scars from a beating administered by her husband, a man she loved and who loved her, for a betrayal she did commit, albeit under pressure from a procuress. The third (the Cateress or Provisioner) is the active one who goes out to market, organises the household, and is the most businesslike. Together they represent three modes of female survival in a patriarchal world: the matriarch who accumulates resources, the romantic who is punished for romanticism, and the practical manager.

**Harun al-Rashid.** The historical Caliph functions as a deus ex machina—hearings, judging, rewarding, punishing. His interest in the stories is simultaneously administrative (he is the guarantor of justice) and personal (he is bored, restless, and curious). His presence in the Ladies' house marks the point where the private world of female domesticity—wine, music, naked bathing, obscene wordplay—is invaded by the patriarchal state.

## 3. Four Passages Worth Quoting

**Passage 1:** The fisherman's lament after the first cast of his net yields a dead jackass:

> "Forbear, O troubles of the world, / And pardon an ye nill forbear: / I went to seek my daily bread / I find that breadless I must fare."

This passage exemplifies Burton's approach to the embedded verse: he renders it in plain English couplets rather than preserving the Arabic monorhyme, which he has described in the Foreword as "monotonous simplicity." The sentiment is Job-like in its directness—man's labour does not guarantee sustenance. But the tone is not despair; the fisherman's next lines suggest a quasi-stoic resignation ("Commit thy needs to Fate and Lot! / Enjoy the Present passing well / And let the Past be clean forgot"). What is striking is the passage's structural placement: it occurs at the lowest ebb of the fisherman's fortunes, the moment before the fourth cast yields the jinni's jar. The verse thus functions as a hinge between绝望 and deliverance, establishing a rhythm—suffering, then strange reversal—that will govern the entire narrative. The prose style around it (simple declarative sentences, direct address) mimics the fisherman's own plainness of mind.

**Passage 2:** The moment the Caliph discovers his wife's infidelity:

> "When King Shahryar saw this infamy of his wife and concubines he became as one distraught and he cried out, 'Only in utter solitude can man be safe from the doings of this vile world!'"

This sentence condenses an enormous emotional range. "As one distraught" is deliberately understated—the prose refuses to elaborate the King's inner state, instead using a comparative phrase that gestures outward toward a universal condition. The spoken line that follows is a generalisation elevated into a principle: the specific injury (his wife's adultery) is translated immediately into a universal theory ("only in utter solitude"). The phrase "vile world" (*dunyá* in Arabic) carries its full theological weight—the world as morally corrupt, as a place of trial rather than satisfaction. The sentence's rhythm is tight and percussive: the alliteration of "vile" and "world," the monosyllabic punch of "Only," the finality of the exclamation mark. It is a thesis statement for the entire tale-cycle.

**Passage 3:** The Lady's description of the Jinniyah who freed her from the sea and transformed her sisters:

> "'I swear by all engraven on the seal-ring of Solomon (with whom be peace!) unless thou deal to each of these bitches three hundred stripes every day I will come and imprison thee for ever under the earth.'"

The passage is a specimen of Burton's treatment of the *saj'a*—the rhymed-prose cadence that runs through the original. The sentence has an almost incantatory quality: the condition ("unless thou… every day"), the quantified threat ("three hundred stripes"), the apocalyptic alternative ("imprison thee for ever under the earth"). The juxtaposition of the devout invocation of Solomon's seal-ring with the brutal counting of lashes enacts exactly what Burton identified as the Nights' central contrast—"quaint element, childish crudities and nursery indecencies and 'vain and amatorious' phrase jostling the finest and highest views of life and character." The Jinniyah's oath is simultaneously an act of supernatural justice (she is protecting the woman who saved her) and an act of systematic torture (her sisters will be beaten daily for an unspecified period). The prose does not resolve this tension; it holds both poles.

**Passage 4:** Shahrazad's first words to Dunyazad on the wedding night:

> "O my sister, an thou be not sleepy, relate to me some new story, delectable and delightsome, the better to speed our waking hours."

This sentence—spoken by the older sister to the younger, inviting the story that will save them both—is a masterpiece of indirection. The phrase "an thou be not sleepy" acknowledges the real circumstances (the wedding night, the hour) while the request for "some new story, delectable and delightsome" converts the danger into a game. "Speed our waking hours" is the operative phrase: the goal is not sleep but waking, not death but survival, and the mechanism is storytelling. The sentence is deceptively simple—short words, domestic register—but it establishes the entire architecture of the work to come: the *alf layla wa layla* structure, the frame-tale methodology, the dependency of the narrative's continuation on the listener's active desire to hear more.

## 4. Themes and How the Prose Builds Them

The text develops several interlocking themes, each reinforced by specific prose strategies.

**Theme 1: The Deception of Appearances.** The Nights is a narrative system built on surfaces that conceal depths. The Caliph travels in merchant's dress; Shahrazad presents herself as a bride but intends to act as a storyteller; the copper jar appears as worthless scrap metal; the beautiful ladies' house conceals a torture chamber; the black bitches are transformed sisters; the magical tarn looks like an ordinary lake. The prose reinforces this at the level of diction: Burton frequently uses phrases like "even so" (*wa-inna kazálika*) to introduce a reversal, and the embedded-tale structure itself—a story within a story within a story—mirrors the epistemological condition of the Nights: you never know which layer is the real one. The prose's periodic insertion of verse into prose, and its alternation between elevated rhymed passages and blunt declarative sentences, enact this doubleness at the formal level.

**Theme 2: The Instability of Fortune and the Power of Intellect.** The fisherman's arc—loss, deeper loss, unexpected salvation—establishes the fundamental rhythmic theorem of the Nights: things can always get worse, and they can always suddenly get better, according to principles opaque to human calculation. The three Kalandars' stories develop this theme by showing three different relationships to Fortune: the First Kalandar's passivity in the face of his cousin's betrayal; the Second Kalandar's intellectual arrogance (kicking the alcove); the Third Kalandar's literal obedience to prophecy (fulfilling it accidentally). Against Fortune's caprice, the text sets the power of the intellect: Shahrazad's storytelling, the fisherman's cunning, Duban's medical knowledge, the Jinniyah's magical learning. The prose strategy here is one of *delayed causation*—the connection between cause and effect is always the last thing revealed, and the pleasure of the narrative depends on this delay. Burton's sentence-length increases dramatically during moments of revelation (as when the fisherman's trick works, or when the Jinniyah explains her history), as if the prose itself were drawing breath
